title: Raga Basant
hook: the raga of spring, and a line about a month when it is always spring

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Bhairao, and your line was the milk offering: Namdev's cup, offered to someone present. A new week starts now.

Somewhere in the Guru Granth Sahib there's a line that does something strange to the calendar. It praises a month, then says that in this month spring is always present. Always. Not for a few weeks between the cold and the heat. A spring that doesn't end. It opens today's raga, Basant, the raga of spring, which tradition sings when the actual spring comes round. So there are two springs in this section. One arrives with the season. The other, the Granth suggests, is something else entirely.
screen: `A MONTH WHEN SPRING IS ALWAYS PRESENT.` → `TWO SPRINGS.` → `RAGA BASANT.`

segments.voice: Basant comes right after Bhairao in the Granth's order. It's also an ordinary word for spring, and the raga carries the season in its name. Tradition sings it in springtime, so here a raga is not only a mood but a calendar: you'd hear these hymns as the fields turn green. The opening hymn, by Guru Nanak, in paraphrase: of all the months, blessed is the month in which spring is always present. Blossom, my mind, by remembering the One. That's the first move. The Guru takes the season everyone waits for, makes it permanent, and hands it to the mind. The second move comes in a hymn by Guru Amar Das further in. In paraphrase: spring has come, and all the green growth has flowered. And these living beings flower too, when they fix their attention on God. Notice the two levels side by side. Outside, a real spring with real blossoms; the hymns don't pretend it isn't lovely. Inside, a flowering that needs no date on the calendar, because it comes from where the mind rests. A field blooms once a year. The Granth's spring is always present, because the One it remembers is always present. So when the season comes round and the gurdwara sings Basant, the outer spring becomes a reminder of the inner one. Today's line is simple: spring.
screen: `BASANT: THE SEASON IN THE NAME.` · `A MONTH WHEN SPRING IS ALWAYS PRESENT.` · `BLOSSOM, MY MIND.` · `THE FIELD BLOOMS; SO DO THE BEINGS.` · then, large: `SPRING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind, or look at, one living thing near you, a plant on the sill, a tree outside, even a weed in a crack of the pavement, and notice that it's growing right now, too slowly to see. Breathe slowly with it, then turn the same attention inward, gently, without forcing anything to bloom. If you pray, remember the One the way Guru Nanak's line asks, blossom, my mind; if you don't, simply rest with the green thing.
Raga Basant. The raga of spring, which follows Bhairao, sung by tradition in the spring season, and opening with Guru Nanak's month in which spring is always present. Today's word.
Your line: spring. In Basant, the inner spring doesn't wait for the season. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In kirtan, shabads from the Basant section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Basant, and tradition gives the raga a special place in the spring season.

chat.says: If Basant is the spring raga, does its message only fit in springtime?
options: No. Guru Nanak speaks of a spring always present: a mind blossoming in remembrance.
Yes. Its hymns are only for spring and make no sense in other seasons.
No, because its hymns say the outer spring is a trap to ignore.
chat.meaning: Basant is sung in spring, but its opening hymn praises a month in which spring is always present: a mind flowering as it remembers the One.
